newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand's baht seen volatile in near term.
newsitem.headline: Thailand's baht seen volatile in near term.

text.p: Thailand's baht, under offshore attack by speculators again on Tuesday, is likely to remain volatile in the near term notwithstanding central bank intervention, analysts said on Tuesday.

In addition to speculation, seasonal factors such as strong dollar demand at the end of the year by corporations to repatriate profits and to square positions would keep the weakened baht on edge, they told Reuters.
"We expect that investors will return to the baht early next year," a dealer at a foreign bank said.

"In part it is a seasonal factor as dollar repatriation flows step up before the year-end. These are much more insistent this year given the widening of the current account deficit...," the London-based I.D.E.A. said in a recent report on the Thai currency's outlook.
Central bank governor Rerngchai Marakanond said on Tuesday he expected the current account deficit for 1996 to be 8.2 percent of gross domestic product compared with 8.1 percent in 1995.
On Tuesday, foreign exchange dealers said speculators attacked the baht to test the limits to which the Thai central bank would go to defend the currency.

It picked up somewhat in late trade in Bangkok after the central bank's intervention in the Singapore market, rising to 25.580/590 from 25.600/605 in the morning. Business was done as low as 25.610/615 early in the day.
Some believed that the Bank of Thailand had spent up to $500 million, selling dollars to prop up the baht. Bank officials declined to comment on the reported intervention.

Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan vowed to stabilise the currency and ruled out any change to the way its value was fixed daily by the central bank against a basket of currencies heavily weighted with the U.S. dollar.
Analysts said a key factor against the baht was investor concern about the slowing Thai economy, weak export growth and a widening current acount deficit.

"Today's baht fall reflects investor concerns about the new government's economic policies. They are waiting for something concrete to emerge," said Charl Kengchon, head of money and banking at Thai Farmers Research Centre Co Ltd.

"Its hard to say where the baht may be headed in the near term, but if the market reacts positively to today's policy statement by Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan, then we will see some improvement," he added.

Other analysts said the central bank's intervention in overseas markets made speculators more cautious and sent a message that the authorities were ready to go quite far to defend and stabilise the baht.
The last time the baht came under speculative attack was in late August and the bank intervened and vowed to defend it.

"I am confident in the Bank of Thailand's ability to control the baht. So there is no reason to believe that the bank would not be in the position to defend the baht," said Ananda P. Bhaumik, a foreign exchange and treasury consultant at Laemthong Bank.
